source_refs.note: Topic 24.2 with Quick Check 24.2, answered (PDF 120-122); the equations are redrawn. The book reduces N-methylethanamide with 'H2' over Ni/Pt in an unbalanced equation; it is balanced here. Answers need review.

items: From halogenoalkanes and ammonia (nucleophilic substitution): CH3CH2Br + NH3 -> CH3CH2NH2 + HBr, with excess ammonia in ethanol under pressure, to avoid secondary amines or a mixture. If ammonia is in excess the main product is the primary amine; if the halogenoalkane is in excess a tertiary amine is the main product.
By reducing nitriles with H2/Ni or LiAlH4: CH3CH2CN + 4[H] -> CH3CH2CH2NH2 (propanenitrile to propan-1-amine).
By reducing nitroalkanes with LiAlH4: CH3CH2NO2 + 6[H] -> CH3CH2NH2 + 2H2O.
By reducing amides with LiAlH4, in good yield: CH3CONH2 + 4[H] -> CH3CH2NH2 + H2O.
By the Hofmann reaction, which gives an amine with one carbon fewer than the amide: CH3CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> CH3NH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O.
By alkylating primary amines: a halogenoalkane heated with a primary amine in ethanol under pressure (in a sealed tube): CH3CH2Br + CH3NH2 -> CH3CH2NHCH3 + HBr.
By reducing N-substituted amides: CH3CONHCH3 + 4[H] -> CH3CH2NHCH3 + H2O.
By ammonolysis of chlorobenzene: C6H5Cl + 2NH3 -> C6H5NH2 + NH4Cl (Cu2O, 250 C, 50 atm).
By reducing nitrobenzene: C6H5NO2 + 6[H] -> C6H5NH2 + 2H2O (Sn and concentrated HCl).
By the Hofmann reaction of benzamide: C6H5CONH2 + Br2 + 4NaOH -> C6H5NH2 + 2NaBr + Na2CO3 + 2H2O.

blocks.alt: Three panels of equations. Aliphatic primary amines: from bromoethane and ammonia, from propanenitrile with LiAlH4, from nitroethane with LiAlH4, from ethanamide with LiAlH4, and by the Hofmann reaction. Aliphatic secondary amines: from bromoethane and methanamine, and by reducing N-methylethanamide. Phenylamine: from chlorobenzene with ammonia, from nitrobenzene with Sn/HCl, and from benzamide by the Hofmann reaction.
blocks.caption: Ways of making amines (original summary of the book's methods).
blocks.long_description: Amines are made either by substitution, with ammonia or an amine as the nucleophile, or by reducing a nitrogen compound (nitrile, nitro compound or amide). The Hofmann reaction is different: it removes the carbonyl carbon, so the amine has one carbon fewer.

blocks.prompt: Suggest a synthesis of 2-phenylethanamine, C6H5CH2CH2NH2 (a 'feel good factor' in chocolate), from chloromethylbenzene, C6H5CH2Cl.
blocks.explanation: Heat C6H5CH2Cl with KCN in ethanol under reflux to get C6H5CH2CN (one more carbon), then reduce the nitrile with LiAlH4 (or H2/Ni): C6H5CH2CN + 4[H] -> C6H5CH2CH2NH2.

blocks.prompt: Which nitro compound, nitrile and amide give (i) the primary amine (CH3)2CHCH2NH2 and (ii) the secondary amine CH3CH2CH2CH2NHCH3 on reduction?
blocks.explanation: (i) Nitro compound (CH3)2CHCH2NO2; nitrile (CH3)2CHCN; amide (CH3)2CHCONH2. (ii) Reducing nitro compounds or nitriles gives only primary amines, so only an amide works: CH3CH2CH2CONHCH3 (N-methylbutanamide).

items: Primary: RX + excess NH3; reduce nitriles, nitro compounds or amides; Hofmann (one C fewer).
Secondary: RX + primary amine; reduce N-substituted amides.
Phenylamine: chlorobenzene + NH3, or reduce nitrobenzene (Sn/HCl).
